```{r}
source("R/helpers.R")
set.seed(STUDENT_SEED)

die_values <- 1:6
population_mean <- mean(die_values)
population_sd <- sqrt(35 / 12)
generator <- function(sample_size) {
  sample(die_values, size = sample_size, replace = TRUE)
}
```

## Question and prediction

The original population is discrete and flat rather than bell-shaped. I expect
the sample means to become smoother and more normal as the sample size grows.
For a fair six-sided die, the theoretical mean is 3.5 and the population
standard deviation is `r round(population_sd, 4)`.

## Original population

```{r}
plot_population_bar(
  sample(die_values, 10000, replace = TRUE),
  "Original six-sided die population",
  "Die value"
)
```

The bar chart shows that the original values are equally likely, but the
population is not continuous and is not bell-shaped.

## Simulation and theoretical comparison

```{r}
means_by_size <- simulate_sample_means(generator)
summary_table <- summarize_sample_means(
  means_by_size,
  theoretical_mean = population_mean,
  theoretical_sd = population_sd
)
print_summary(summary_table)
first_screened_n <- summary_table$sample_size[summary_table$screening_rule][1]
chosen_row <- summary_table[summary_table$sample_size == first_screened_n, , drop = FALSE]
```

## Sample sizes investigated

I investigated sample sizes `n = 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, and 200`. I used
small values first because a die produces a discrete population, and I wanted
to see how quickly averaging would smooth it out. I also included `n = 30`
because it is a common classroom rule and included larger values for comparison.

For each sample size, the simulated standard deviation of the means can be
compared with `population_sd / sqrt(n)`. The comparison helps check whether the
simulation agrees with the CLT's standard-error prediction.

## Visual evidence

```{r}
selected_sizes <- c(2, 5, 10, 30)
plot_selected_diagnostics(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Six-sided die")
plot_selected_qq(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Six-sided die Q-Q plot")
```

The smallest sample sizes can show visible discreteness because only certain
averages are possible. With larger samples, the possible averages are closer
together and the overall shape should become more bell-like.

## Approximate normal decision

My final answer is **n =** `r first_screened_n`. At this sample size, the
histogram was more bell-shaped than it was for the smaller values, and the Q-Q
plot was reasonably close to a straight line. The skewness was
`r round(chosen_row$skewness, 3)`, the excess kurtosis was
`r round(chosen_row$excess_kurtosis, 3)`, and the simulated standard deviation
was `r round(chosen_row$simulated_sd, 4)` compared with a theoretical standard
error of `r round(chosen_row$theoretical_se, 4)`.

The first sample means are still somewhat discrete because they can only take
certain values. As `n` increases, the possible averages become closer
together. The results show that a discrete population can still have
approximately normal sample means.

## What surprised me

I was surprised that the die's sample means became approximately normal with a
fairly small sample size, even though the original population was not
continuous and was not bell-shaped.
